blocks.content: The how-data-travels topic, back in the Networking Fundamentals module, introduced the idea that a packet hops from router to router on its way to a destination, like asking for directions repeatedly along a road trip. This topic goes much deeper: exactly how a router actually decides where to send a packet next.

This is not a small detail buried inside networking, routing decisions made correctly, quickly, and consistently across millions of routers is a huge part of what actually makes the internet work at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015510436-989770927.png
blocks.alt: A packet hops from router to router on its way to a destination, each router making its own forwarding decision

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015512318-644717319.png
blocks.alt: How data travels introduced the hop by hop journey; this topic covers exactly how each individual hop decision gets made

blocks.content: 1. The Routing Table: Every Router's Decision Guide
blocks.text: 1. The Routing Table: Every Router's Decision Guide

blocks.content: Every router maintains a routing table, a list of known destination address ranges and which direction, which outgoing interface, to send a packet toward for each one. When a packet arrives, the router checks this table to decide exactly where to forward it next.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015513936-280664220.png
blocks.alt: A routing table maps destination address ranges to the outgoing interface a packet should be sent toward

blocks.content: 2. Longest Prefix Match: Choosing the Most Specific Route
blocks.text: 2. Longest Prefix Match: Choosing the Most Specific Route

blocks.content: Sometimes a single destination address genuinely matches more than one entry in the routing table at once, tying directly back to the CIDR topic address range notation. When this happens, the router always picks the MORE SPECIFIC match, the entry with the longer prefix, the smaller, more precisely targeted range, rather than the broader, more general one.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015515832-255914287.png
blocks.alt: When multiple entries match a destination, the router always chooses the more specific, longer prefix match

blocks.title: Why the more specific route wins
blocks.content: A more specific entry represents a more precise, deliberately configured piece of knowledge about that exact destination range. The router trusts that specificity over a broader, more general fallback whenever both genuinely apply.
3. Static Versus Dynamic Routing

Static routing means a human manually configures the routing table entries by hand, simple and predictable, but it does not adapt at all if the network itself changes, a link going down, for instance. Dynamic routing instead has routers automatically communicate with each other, sharing information about what they can reach and how, and adjusting their own tables in response to real changes.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015517382-392173813.png
blocks.alt: Static routing is manually configured and fixed; dynamic routing automatically adapts as the network itself changes

4. The Default Route: A Catch All Fallback
blocks.text: 4. The Default Route: A Catch All Fallback

blocks.content: If a destination address does not match any specific entry in the routing table at all, it falls through to the default route, a catch all entry that typically points toward the wider internet. This is exactly why a home router default route usually just points at your internet provider, sending anything not specifically known locally onward toward the broader internet.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015518997-100992350.png
blocks.alt: A destination matching no specific entry falls through to the default route, typically pointing toward the wider internet

blocks.content: 5. Each Router Only Knows the Next Hop
blocks.text: 5. Each Router Only Knows the Next Hop

blocks.content: A genuinely important, sometimes surprising detail: an individual router does not know the entire remaining path a packet will take to its final destination. It only knows, from its own routing table, which direction is the right NEXT hop. Every single router along the way makes this exact same kind of local, independent decision, one hop at a time.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015520675-121711658.png
blocks.alt: Each router only knows the correct next hop from its own table, not the entire remaining path to the destination

blocks.content: 6. The Road Trip Analogy, Revisited

Asking for directions repeatedly along a road trip captures this precisely, and directly extends the analogy already used in the how-data-travels topic. Each local person you ask only tells you the next landmark to head toward, not the entire remaining route to your final destination. Following each hint in turn, one hop at a time, eventually gets you there, exactly like a packet hopping router to router.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784015522183-676378926.png
blocks.alt: Asking for directions repeatedly, one landmark at a time, mirrors exactly how a packet is routed hop by hop

blocks.content: 7. Why This Design Makes the Internet Resilient
blocks.text: 7. Why This Design Makes the Internet Resilient

blocks.content: Because each router makes its own independent, local decision based on current conditions, if one specific path or link goes down, dynamic routing can automatically recalculate a different next hop and route around the failure entirely. No single router needs to know or plan the entire end to end path in advance for this resilience to work.

blocks.title: A direct callback to how-data-travels
blocks.content: This is exactly the resilience the how-data-travels topic pointed to when it explained why different packets belonging to the same message can take genuinely different paths, each router making its own current, independent decision is precisely what makes that flexibility possible.
8. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

["Assuming a router plans the entire end to end path a packet will take, when it actually only ever decides the single correct next hop, one router at a time.","Assuming the broadest matching routing table entry is always used, when the router specifically prefers the most specific, longest prefix match available.","Every router maintains its own routing table mapping destinations to outgoing directions.","Longest prefix match means the more specific entry always wins when several match.","Static routing is manually configured; dynamic routing automatically adapts to real changes.","The default route is the catch all fallback for anything not specifically known."]

Assuming the broadest matching routing table entry is always used, when the router specifically prefers the most specific, longest prefix match available.
Every router maintains its own routing table mapping destinations to outgoing directions.
Longest prefix match means the more specific entry always wins when several match.

The default route is the catch all fallback for anything not specifically known.
